view.text:
11:47 PM. The storm has been working at the windows for an hour.

Across the hall, 6D is dark. It has been dark most nights since March. Since the night Teo knocked on your door at two in the morning, and you stood on this side of it and didn't answer. The police came later. You never asked him why.

Someone knocks. Three times, evenly, the way people knock when they already know you're home.

Through the peephole: a woman in a dark coat, soaked through, hair flat against her face. She isn't shivering. She is looking straight into the lens, as if she can see you on the other side of it.

"Please," she says. "You already let me in."

You have never seen her before. Your hand is on the deadbolt. In your pocket, your thumb finds the folded receipt. You've never been able to get rid of it.

You turn the deadbolt. It is loud in the narrow entry, louder than it should be.

On the other side of the door, nothing. No knock. No footsteps. Then, softly, almost kindly:

"That's all right. You did, though."

Water runs out from under the door in a thin, straight line, as if it has somewhere to be.

Your hand stays on the lock. You know this feeling. You had it in March.

She crosses the hall to 6D and knocks. Teo's door. Teo, who hasn't opened his door to anyone since March. Not the super. Not you.

For a moment the chain lifts. Then it drops again. You know how long a person can stand behind a door without answering.

She says something to the wood that you can't hear.

Then she walks to the stairwell, and the fire door sighs shut behind her. Down. Not up. You can hear her going down for a long time.

The lights go out at 11:58. The fridge stops humming, and in the quiet you hear the building the way you never do: pipes, wind in the elevator shaft, something settling in the walls.

You sit on the floor with your back against the locked door, because it seems like the only fixed thing in the apartment.

Somewhere far below, a metal door closes. Then, very faintly, someone laughs.

It sounds like you.

view.text:
At 12:06 there is a sound at Teo's door: the chain, the bolt, the chain again. It opens two inches. One eye. A strip of grey cardigan.

"She was in there," he says. "With you. I heard her in your apartment."

You start to tell him that's impossible, that your door has been locked all night.

"I heard you lock it," he says. "I heard you open it, too. I always hear you." A pause. "I heard you in March. On the other side of the door."

He looks toward the stairwell. "She went down. If you trust me, don't. Go up. Up is just weather."

The door closes. The chain.

The roof door sticks, then gives, and the storm takes the breath out of you. The city is dark to the river. The whole grid, not just your building. Water stands on the tar in sheets.

You are alone up here. You are sure of that for almost a minute.

Below the parapet, one window on the sixth floor is open to the storm. 6D. Teo is leaning out of it, looking up at you, rain in his face.

"I wasn't asking you to save me," he calls. "In March. I just needed somebody else to hear it."

"Four numbers," he calls. "I heard her say them, through the wall. In the other night. They open 07." The window closes.

Then the stairwell door bangs shut behind you, though nobody came through it.

view.text:
Three knocks. Behind you. The door to the stairwell isn't the stairwell door any more.

The same paint as yours. The same brass peephole. The same scratch beside the lock.

Your door.

You put your eye to the peephole.

Someone is standing on the other side, soaked through. Your coat. Your hands. Your face.

For a second you think it's a mirror.

Then the person blinks.

You didn't.

view.text:
"I know what you chose," they say. It's your voice, from the wrong side of the wood.

"I opened it. I let her in."

"She took the folded receipt out of my hand and wrote 1011 on it. I let her."

They try the handle. It doesn't move. They put a palm flat against the door. You can hear them breathing. Exactly as you are.

"I would have opened it for Teo, too."

"Why do you get to be the real one?"

They're waiting.

Lock it, and the other you is gone. You won't have to hear them again.

Open it, and they come in. Neither of you knows what happens when two versions of one life meet.

changed: The brass key is at your feet. And it is in Mara's hand, beside you. You can feel both, like holding one thing in two hands.
Your folded receipt is in your hand. It always was.
Mara is in the basement. She is also beside you; you can hear her, and she can hear herself. She doesn't look surprised.
view.text:
You turn the deadbolt. It is loud in the narrow entry, louder than it should be.

Through the peephole, the other you goes still. You know that expression. It's the face you make when you know no one is coming.

"1011" fades from the folded receipt, and "STAY HERE" from the key's paper tag, like breath off a mirror, and then there is nothing left to read.

Far below, a metal door closes, gently, and does not open again.

At 12:30 every light in the building comes back at once, and the fridge begins to hum as if nothing happened.

Then, three knocks. Slow. Patient.

You don't move until they stop.

Somewhere, you made a different choice.
